strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: universal, transferable, black-box patch attacks on VLA-driven robots, which has direct safety relevance for embodied AI deployment.

The framework is technically comprehensive, combining a feature-space L1/contrastive objective, a robustness-augmented (min-max) patch optimization inspired by adversarially-trained surrogate transfer literature, and two novel VLA-specific losses (Patch Attention Dominance and Patch Semantic Misalignment) that target cross-modal attention and instruction grounding rather than only pixel-level perturbation.

The paper provides a theoretical motivation (Assumption 1, Proposition 1, Corollary 1) linking surrogate-side feature deviations to target-side deviations, giving some principled justification for the design choices, and supports it empirically with CCA/linear-probe evidence of shared representational structure.

Thorough ablation studies (Table 3, Table 4) isolate the contribution of each loss term (RUPA, PAD, PSM, Jtr components) and text-probe design, showing that most components contribute non-trivially to transfer performance.

Qualitative patch analysis (Fig. 2) shows the proposed patches avoid surrogate/embodiment-specific textures (e.g., gripper mimicry) seen in baseline methods, supporting the claim of more model-agnostic, transferable perturbations.

Evaluation spans multiple task suites (LIBERO Spatial/Object/Goal/Long) and multiple victim models (OpenVLA-oft variants, OpenVLA-oft-w, mention of π0), providing reasonably broad coverage for the black-box transfer claims made in the main text.
weaknesses: Numerous appendix references are broken ("Appendix ??") throughout the paper, meaning several claims central to the paper's argument—white-box performance, transfer results to π0 (the most architecturally distinct victim and the strongest test of the universality claim), and even the proof of Proposition 1—are asserted but not verifiable in the submitted manuscript.

The distinction between "Simulated" and "Physical" columns in Tables 1-2 is unclear and potentially misleading: both appear to report LIBERO (simulator) success rates against different training-data checkpoints (LIBERO-Long-trained vs. BridgeData V2-trained models) rather than actual physical robot trials, despite the title ("When Robots Obey the Patch") and abstract explicitly claiming "physical executions" and real-world validation. This terminology should be clarified or the physical-world claims should be tempered.

The linear-alignment assumption (Assumption 1) underlying the theoretical justification is a strong simplification of the relationship between very different VLA architectures (e.g., autoregressive OpenVLA vs. flow-based π-series), and the supporting empirical evidence (a single R²≈0.654 value) is reported without sufficient methodological detail (which layers, which model pair, which data) to assess its generality.

The reported effectiveness of the proposed method varies substantially across victim/setting combinations (e.g., near-complete task failure in Table 1 simulated at 5.75% average success vs. only moderate degradation to 61.5% in Table 2 physical), which somewhat undercuts the "universal" framing and is not thoroughly discussed or explained beyond noting a "larger distribution and policy gap."

No defense or countermeasure evaluation is provided despite the paper positioning itself as "establishing a strong baseline for future defenses"; without at least a basic defense/detection baseline, this claim is unsupported by evidence in the manuscript.

Baseline comparison is limited to a single prior work's six objective variants (RoboticAttack); broader comparison with other transfer-based or feature-space adversarial patch methods from the general (non-VLA) adversarial robustness literature discussed in Related Work is absent, limiting the strength of the comparative claims.

Implementation details necessary for reproducibility (patch size/area budget, hyperparameters α, β, λ weights, number of probe phrases, training schedule) are deferred to the missing appendix, making it difficult to assess or reproduce the method from the main text alone.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: universal, black-box transferable patch attacks on VLA-driven robots, rather than white-box, single-model overfit patches.

The framework combines several technically motivated components (ℓ1 feature deviation with a supporting theoretical bound, repulsive InfoNCE regularization, a bi-level robustness-augmentation scheme, and two VLA-specific losses for attention hijacking and semantic misalignment) into a coherent pipeline rather than an ad hoc combination.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across multiple LIBERO task suites, multiple OpenVLA-oft fine-tuned variants, and a stated architecturally different target (π0), which stresses cross-recipe and cross-architecture transfer more than prior work.
Ablation studies (Tables 3-4) probe the marginal contribution of each loss term and of the text-probe design, giving some insight into which components matter most.

Qualitative patch visualization analysis is a nice touch, showing that baseline patches tend to mimic scene/robot-specific textures (overfitting) while the proposed patch stays more abstract/feature-driven.
weaknesses: Nearly all key supporting material is missing from the manuscript as submitted: the proof of Proposition 1, implementation details, white-box results, and the π0 transfer results are all referenced only via broken "Appendix ??" pointers with no appendix content provided, making several central claims (including the crucial cross-architecture π0 transfer result touted in the abstract/intro) unverifiable in this submission.

The theoretical justification (Assumption 1: a single global linear map relating surrogate and target features) is a strong assumption for models that the paper itself describes as differing "fundamentally... in backbone choice, pretraining/fine-tuning data, and training strategy" (e.g., OpenVLA vs. π0); the reported R² ≈ 0.654 is only moderate and is measured for a single (unspecified) pair, undermining generality of the bound used to motivate the ℓ1 objective.

The paper's title and framing ("When Robots Obey the Patch," "physical patch," "sim-to-real shifts") strongly suggest real hardware deployment, but no actual physical robot experiments, photographs, or videos are shown; the "Physical" columns in Tables 1-2 appear to refer to models trained on the real-world BridgeData V2 dataset evaluated via rollout, not an actual physical execution with a printed patch under real lighting/viewpoint variation — this risks overclaiming the practical/physical-world validity of the attack.

The ablation in Table 3 shows removing the robustness-augmented component (w/o RUPA) barely changes performance (62.25 vs. 61.50 average), which is inconsistent with the paper's emphasis on RAUP/RUPA as a major contribution and raises doubts about its actual necessity.

Results are somewhat inconsistent across settings: in several categories (e.g., "long" task success in Table 2), baseline methods already reduce success to near-floor levels comparable to the proposed method, so the claimed superiority is driven largely by a subset of categories/tasks rather than uniform improvement.

No variance/error bars are reported despite the stochastic patch placement and transformation sampling used during both training and evaluation, making it hard to assess whether reported gaps are statistically meaningful.

The related work section cites at least one closely related paper on model-agnostic adversarial attack/defense for VLA models ([57]) without a direct empirical or conceptual comparison, weakening the "first universal, transferable patch attack framework for VLA robotics" novelty claim.

No analysis of patch detectability/stealth or robustness against simple defenses (e.g., input transformation, patch detection, adversarial training counters), limiting the paper's usefulness as a benchmark for defense research despite claiming to establish such a baseline.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: universal, transferable adversarial patches for VLA robots under black-box conditions, rather than the white-box, single-model setting used in most prior work (e.g., RoboticAttack).

Provides a principled theoretical motivation (Assumption 1 on linear feature alignment, Proposition 1, Corollary 1) that connects the choice of an ℓ1 feature-deviation objective to guaranteed lower-bounded displacement on an unseen target model, giving the design a justification beyond pure heuristics.

The robustness-augmented bi-level optimization (inner sample-wise perturbation, outer universal patch) is a creative way to approximate the benefits of adversarially-trained surrogates for transfer without the prohibitive cost of adversarially training a large VLA.

Two well-motivated VLA-specific losses (Patch Attention Dominance and Patch Semantic Misalignment) target mechanisms specific to VLA architectures (cross-modal attention and instruction grounding) rather than simply reusing classifier-style attacks, which is a meaningful methodological contribution.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation spanning multiple VLA families (OpenVLA, OpenVLA-oft variants, π0), multiple LIBERO task suites, and ablations isolating the contribution of each loss term and design choice (Tables 3 and 4), which supports the claimed universality.

Qualitative patch analysis (Fig. 2) meaningfully illustrates that baseline patches overfit to scene/embodiment cues (e.g., gripper-like textures) while the proposed patch avoids this, supporting the transferability narrative with an interpretable signal beyond aggregate numbers.
weaknesses: The manuscript as provided has multiple unresolved 'Appendix ??' references (white-box results, proof of Proposition 1, implementation/hyperparameter details, π0 transfer results), leaving core claims (e.g., the hardest cross-family transfer to π0) unverifiable from the main text alone.

The linear alignment assumption underlying the theoretical justification is supported by only a single, fairly weak empirical check (R²≈0.654 for one surrogate/target pair); it is unclear how well this assumption holds across the broader set of surrogate–victim pairs actually used in the experiments, undermining the generality of the theoretical motivation.

The distinction between 'Simulated' and 'Physical' settings in Tables 1–2 is unclear: both use LIBERO-style task categories (spatial/object/goal/long) and success-rate evaluation, raising the question of whether 'Physical' genuinely denotes real-world robot hardware trials or merely a different training-data source evaluated in simulation; if the latter, the abstract's claim of 'physical executions' may overstate the experimental scope.

No evaluation against existing or plausible defenses (e.g., patch detection, input transformation/randomization, adversarial training) is presented, despite the paper positioning itself as 'a strong baseline for future defenses'; without any defense results, the practical security implications are only partially substantiated.

The magnitude of improvement over baselines is very large in some conditions (e.g., 5.75% vs. 41–69% average success for competitors), which is a striking result that would benefit from additional scrutiny (e.g., matched patch size/area budget, statistical variance across seeds/trials) to rule out evaluation asymmetries between the proposed method and baselines.

Results are reported as single-run success rates without variance/confidence intervals across the 10 trials per task or across different random seeds for patch training, limiting assessment of statistical robustness of the reported gains.

The overall pipeline combines many components and hyperparameters (λcon, λPAD, λPSM, PGD budget, probe-phrase choices, etc.), and with implementation details deferred to an unavailable appendix, reproducibility from the main text alone is limited.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored gap: most prior VLA adversarial-patch work assumes white-box access to a single victim, while this paper targets universal, transferable, black-box patch attacks with a systematic framework (UPA-RFAS).

The methodology combines multiple well-motivated components tailored to VLA architecture: a feature-space l1+contrastive objective grounded in a linear-alignment assumption with a supporting proposition/corollary, a robustness-augmented bi-level (inner PGD / outer patch) optimization inspired by robust-surrogate transfer literature, and two VLA-specific losses (attention hijacking and semantic misalignment) that go beyond generic feature attacks.
Reasonably thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each loss term, patch size, contrastive weight, and the inner perturbation budget, which helps interpret the design choices.

Qualitative real-world robot demonstrations and patch-pattern visualizations (Fig. 2) that contrast the proposed feature-space patch against baseline object-mimicking patches, offering some intuition for why the method transfers better.
The paper reports both white-box and black-box results and includes cross-family transfer to a structurally different VLA (π0), which is a meaningful and difficult transfer setting.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification (Assumption 1: linear alignment between surrogate and target feature spaces) is only loosely validated by a single R²≈0.654 regression-probe number and unspecified residual bound εE; this is a fairly weak empirical basis for a claim underpinning the entire framework's transferability guarantee, and no evidence is given that this assumption holds across the diverse victim models actually tested.

The 'universal transferable' claim is only strongly supported for OpenVLA→OpenVLA-oft transfer, which is a fine-tuned variant of the same base architecture rather than a genuinely different model family; transfer to the structurally distinct π0 model (Table 5) shows only modest degradation (e.g., 92%→86% simulated, 92%→83.5% physical), which is far less convincing evidence of true architecture-agnostic universality than the headline numbers suggest.

The experimental setup description for 'Simulated' vs 'Physical' settings in Table 1 is confusing: it is unclear how a model trained on real-world BridgeData v2 is evaluated on LIBERO spatial/object/goal/long task suites, since these are simulation-specific tasks; this ambiguity makes it hard to verify what is actually being measured as 'physical' performance and raises concerns about experimental rigor/clarity.
Real-world physical validation is purely qualitative (3 trials × 3 tasks, no quantitative success-rate statistics), which is insufficient to substantiate claims of practical real-world threat.

In the white-box setting (Table 4/Appendix C), several baseline objectives (e.g., UADA1−3) achieve equal or stronger attack success than the proposed method, which is only briefly acknowledged; this partially undercuts the narrative that the proposed objective is uniformly superior.

Ablations and analysis are conducted almost exclusively against a single victim (OpenVLA-oft); it is unclear whether the same component-wise conclusions (e.g., importance of PAD/PSM/RUPA) hold for the more distant π0 victim, limiting confidence in the generality of the design choices.
The paper does not compare against or discuss any adversarial-patch defenses or provide guidance on detectability, despite claiming to establish 'a baseline for future defenses.'

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: universal, transferable, black-box adversarial patch attacks against VLA-driven robots, going beyond prior white-box-only patch attacks (e.g., RoboticAttack).

The proposed UPA-RFAS framework is technically creative, combining a feature-space l1/contrastive objective with two VLA-specific losses (Patch Attention Dominance and Patch Semantic Misalignment) that are reasonably well motivated by the architecture of VLA models (text→vision attention, image-text alignment).

Theoretical justification (Proposition 1/Corollary 1) gives a principled, if simplified, argument for why increasing surrogate-side l1 feature deviation should induce target-side deviation under a linear alignment assumption.

Extensive ablations (patch size, lambda_con, RUPA epsilon, text-probe phrasing) help clarify the contribution of each design choice and show internal consistency with the paper's own narrative (e.g., Lcon shaping direction vs L1 shaping magnitude).

Evaluates across a reasonably large set of victim models (multiple OpenVLA-oft variants, pi0), tasks (LIBERO suites), and simulated/physical settings, which is more comprehensive than many prior single-model patch-attack papers.
weaknesses: The core empirical claim of strong transfer to fundamentally different VLA architectures is only weakly supported: against pi0 (Table 5), the proposed method's advantage over baselines is marginal (e.g., 86.00 vs 88.50 simulated avg, 83.50 vs 89.00 physical avg), undermining the paper's central claim of markedly superior universal transferability when the surrogate/victim gap is largest.

Real-world physical validation is extremely limited: only three tasks run three times each, reported purely qualitatively with no quantitative success-rate table for actual hardware trials, which is insufficient evidence for the strong real-world threat claims made in the abstract and conclusion.

Only one surrogate direction (OpenVLA-7B as source) is tested; the paper never shows transfer starting from a different family of surrogate (e.g., pi0 or OpenVLA-oft as source), so the 'universal' claim is asymmetric and not fully substantiated.

The attack's effectiveness is highly sensitive to patch size (Table 6: 3% patch is nearly ineffective while 10% nearly fully disables the policy), suggesting that much of the reported degradation may be driven by sheer visible patch area rather than the proposed transferable-feature mechanism; this interacts with practicality claims about physical patches.

Assumption 1 (shared linear subspace across VLA policies), which underlies the theoretical motivation, is validated with only a single aggregate statistic (R^2 ≈ 0.654 and unspecified top-k CCA values) without details on how/where this was measured, which models, or how robust this holds across different victim families; this is thin empirical support for a formal assumption central to the paper's framing.

The method underperforms several baselines in the white-box setting (Appendix C, e.g., UPA and TMA having notably different rankings), and while the authors argue this is expected given the transfer-focused design, it somewhat weakens the overall narrative of a uniformly stronger attack.

The text-probe design for PSM relies on manually curated action/direction phrases; the ablation (Table 3) shows large performance swings depending on this hand-crafted vocabulary, raising concerns about overfitting to the chosen probe set and limited generality to other instruction styles/languages.

No evaluation against existing or plausible defenses (e.g., patch detection, input transformation, robust training) is provided, despite claims that the work 'establishes a baseline for future defenses'; the absence of any defense-side experiments makes this claim largely aspirational.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation (e.g., overloaded symbols across sections) and the paper would benefit from more intuitive explanation of why each loss term specifically helps VLA-relevant failure modes, beyond the formal derivations.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: universal, transferable, black-box patch attacks on VLA-driven robots, which is more practically relevant than the white-box patch attacks studied in prior work (e.g., RoboticAttack).

The framework is well-motivated by an explicit theoretical link (Assumption 1, Proposition 1, Corollary 1) between surrogate-side and target-side feature deviations, giving a principled justification for the ℓ1 deviation objective, supported empirically with CCA and linear-probe R^2 analysis.

The design combines complementary signals (feature-space ℓ1+contrastive, attention hijacking via PAD, semantic misalignment via PSM, and a robustness-augmented bi-level optimization) that are individually motivated and empirically validated via ablation (Table 2), showing each component contributes to transfer.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple victim architectures with different fine-tuning recipes (OpenVLA-oft, OpenVLA-oft-w) and a structurally different backbone (π0), across both simulated and 'physical'-trained models, and across four LIBERO task suites, demonstrating consistently stronger black-box degradation than several strong baselines.

Useful auxiliary analyses: patch-size sensitivity, hyperparameter ablations (λcon, ϵ in RUPA), text-probe phrasing ablation, and qualitative patch-pattern comparison showing the proposed patch avoids object/embodiment-specific mimicry unlike baselines.
Includes a qualitative real-robot demonstration in addition to simulated/dataset-based evaluation, showing some evidence of practical applicability beyond simulation.
weaknesses: The distinction between 'Simulated' and 'Physical' settings in the main quantitative tables (e.g., Table 1) is not clearly defined in the main text — it appears 'Physical' refers to a model trained on real-world BridgeData V2 but still evaluated via rollouts rather than an actual robot, which is confusingly different from the qualitative real-world trials in Appendix F (only 3 tasks x 3 trials, no baseline comparison, no quantitative success rate). This blurs the paper's central claim of 'physical execution' transfer.

The theoretical justification (Assumption 1, linear alignment) is only moderately supported empirically: R^2 ≈ 0.654 for the linear probe is not particularly high, meaning a substantial portion of target-side feature variance is not explained by the assumed linear map, which weakens the rigor of the transferability guarantee built on top of it.

All surrogate experiments use only OpenVLA-derived models (OpenVLA-7B and its LIBERO-Long variant); the paper never demonstrates surrogate diversity (e.g., a non-OpenVLA surrogate), so claims of general 'model-agnostic' transfer rest entirely on the victim side, leaving open whether the specific surrogate family biases the learned universal directions.

No comparison to or discussion of applying existing defenses (adversarial training on VLAs, patch detection/removal, smoothing) despite the paper positioning itself as 'a baseline for future defenses'; this limits the completeness of the security assessment.

The code repository link is left blank/placeholder, and given the complexity of the pipeline (bi-level optimization, attention/semantic loss computation across model-specific internals), reproducibility relies heavily on the released code that is not verifiably available at submission time.

Patch size used in main results (5%, with an ablation up to 10%) is relatively large and visually conspicuous for a 'patch' attack, raising questions about stealthiness/practicality claims relative to smaller, more classically 'patch-like' adversarial perturbations.

Table 1 (the main transfer results) lacks variance/standard deviation across trials, unlike Tables 4 and 5, making it harder to assess the statistical reliability of the reported success-rate drops, especially for close comparisons (e.g., ablation differences of a few percentage points in Table 2).
